name: FastPFor (FastPFOR C++ library)
baseline: Simple-8b and VByte (as measured in the TurboPFor README table)
workload: Same TurboPFor icapp ZIPF benchmark (100M Zipfian integers): FP_SimdFastPFor 64Ki block decode vs Simple-8b and FP_VByte
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'can decode at least 4 billions of compressed integers per second ... 15 GB/s', 'significantly faster than generic codecs like gzip, LZO, Snappy or LZ4'. Third-party table (TurboPFor README, ZIPF): FP_SimdFastPFor 8748 MB/s decode vs Simple-8b 3832 (~2.3x, derived from page data) and vs FP_VByte 4268 (~2.0x, derived from page data); encode 624 MB/s is slower than Simple-8b 848.
stars_or_usage: 978 stars; DuckDB derived code from it; Lucene 4.6 PForDelta format derived from FastPFOR
tradeoffs: Research library for 32-bit integers (64-bit coverage is partial); SSSE3 minimum for key codecs, NEON on aarch64; no input validation during decode (documented); best codecs need 128-integer or larger blocks (FastPFor itself needs larger blocks than SIMD binary packing).
caveats: The repo README claims are against gzip/LZO/Snappy/LZ4 (not in the baseline list). The Simple-8b and VByte comparison is derived from a competitor's table that gives no flags; encode speed of SimdFastPFor is lower than Simple-8b in that table. The SPE 2015 paper 'Decoding billions of integers per second through vectorization' (peer reviewed, seen only as a WebSearch snippet because arXiv and Wiley were blocked) is the primary evidence and was not opened. Note FastPFor is itself the baseline other catalog entries beat.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ SIMD integer compression bit packing faster than FastPFor varint github'; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: MaskedVByte
workload: TurboPFor ZIPF and gov2.sorted decode of VByte-compressed integers, single thread
claimed_speedup: Third-party table: ZIPF MaskedVByte 6689 MB/s encode / 9524 decode vs FP_VByte 5200 / 4268 and PC_Vbyte 2260 / 4208 (derived from page data: ~2.2x decode vs FP_VByte); gov2 MaskedVByte 2740 / 3384 vs FP_Vbyte 1888 / 1980 (~1.7x decode, ~1.5x encode derived).
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; integrated into Apache Lucene experiments and PISA
tradeoffs: Decodes the standard VByte format, so it is format-compatible with ordinary varint; needs SSE4.1 or NEON; 32-bit integers only.
caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); README table gives no CPU or flags (the README links an issue titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2' whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags), and the table is labelled 2019.11. The repo README itself has no numbers; the paper (Plaisance, Kurz, Lemire, 'Vectorized VByte Decoding', 2015) is on arXiv, which was blocked, so it was not opened.
found_via: Listed in the FastPFor and TurboPFor READMEs; opened github.com/lemire/MaskedVByte

name: simdcomp
workload: gov2.sorted docid set, block 128 with delta coding, single thread (TurboPFor README table row SC_SIMDPack128)
claimed_speedup: Third-party table: SC_SIMDPack128 6952 MB/s encode / 9488 MB/s decode vs Simple-8b 836 / 3296 and FP_Vbyte 1888 / 1980 (derived from page data: ~8.3x encode and ~2.9x decode vs Simple-8b; ~3.7x and ~4.8x vs FP_Vbyte). Compression ratio 21.8% vs Simple-8b 18.9%. Repo README: 'decode at least 4 billions of compressed integers per second' and '0.3 cycles per integer on a Skylake'.
stars_or_usage: 538 stars; used by upscaledb, EventQL, ManticoreSearch
tradeoffs: Binary packing of 128-integer blocks, so worse compression than Simple-8b / PFor on skewed data; needs SSE2/SSE4.1 or NEON; C API usable from C++; the 128-block unit is bad for short arrays (LittleIntPacker targets that).
caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); README table gives no CPU or flags (the README links an issue titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2' whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags), and the table is labelled 2019.11. The repo's own bitpackingbenchmark reports cycles per integer but the README gives no baseline comparison; the 15 GB/s claim compares to gzip/LZO/Snappy/LZ4.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github lemire streamvbyte simdcomp SIMD-BP128 integer compression library'; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

compiler_and_flags: Release build via CMake; compiler and flags not stated
name: SIMDCompressionAndIntersection
workload: vteromero shootout on gov2.sorted, delta-coded sorted 32-bit integer lists, i7-6700HQ; the library supplies the Delta+BinaryPacking, Delta+FastPFor and Delta+VariableByte codecs
claimed_speedup: Shootout row Delta+BinaryPacking 2.30 G/s encode / 2.33 G/s decode vs Delta+VariableByte 1.62 / 1.52 and Delta+FastPFor128 615.66 M/s (derived from page data: ~1.4x / ~1.5x vs VByte, ~3.7x vs FastPFor128). Repo README: 'decode at least 4 billions of compressed integers per second ... 15 GB/s'.
tradeoffs: C++11 library for sorted lists with SIMD differential coding plus SIMD set-intersection routines; SSE2 required, SSE4.1 for some codecs; pre-sorted input expected for the delta schemes.
caveats: The shootout's 'BinaryPacking' row may be the scalar variant rather than SIMDBinaryPacking (not confirmed); the shootout is by the author of a competing codec (VTEnc). The library overlaps with FastPFor and simdcomp code, which are listed separately. Compiler flags unstated.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/integer-compression?l=c%2B%2B; benchmark from vteromero/integer-compression-benchmarks

hardware: Skylake i7-6700 (TurboPFor issue #47) for the competitor table; Apple M4 Max for the repo's own numbers
name: StreamVByte
baseline: VByte / varint (FP_VByte, PC_Vbyte) and Google Group Varint
workload: TurboPFor ZIPF (100M integers, 0..255 skew) and gov2.sorted; encode/decode MB/s, single thread, 'Streamvbyte 2019' row
claimed_speedup: Third-party table: ZIPF StreamVbyte 11197 MB/s encode / 11984 decode vs FP_VByte 5200 / 4268 (derived from page data: ~2.2x encode, ~2.8x decode); gov2 StreamVbyte 8456 / 9476 vs FP_Vbyte 1888 / 1980 (~4.5x, ~4.8x derived). Repo README: ~27 GB/s encode, ~41 GB/s decode (mixed 1-4 byte) on an Apple M4 Max, no baseline in that table.
stars_or_usage: 419 stars; used by RediSearch, StarRocks, Facebook Thrift, upscaledb, tilemaker
tradeoffs: Byte-aligned, so compression ratio is worse than bit-packing (31.2% on ZIPF vs 25.0% for TurboPack); decoder may read STREAMVBYTE_PADDING bytes past input; SSE4.1 / NEON with runtime dispatch and scalar fallback.
caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); README table gives no CPU or flags (the README links an issue titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2' whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags), and the table is labelled 2019.11. Newer StreamVByte code (version 3.0.0, April 2026) differs from the '2019' build in the table. The competitor repo also claims TurboByte is faster than StreamVByte (issue #96, no CPU or flags stated).
found_via: WebSearch: 'github lemire streamvbyte simdcomp SIMD-BP128 integer compression library'; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

hardware: Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz (stated only in linked issue #47 title/body, not in the table)
name: TurboPFor Integer Compression
workload: icapp benchmark on 100M Zipfian integers (block 128/256) and the gov2.sorted docid set, single thread, encode and decode MB/s
claimed_speedup: ZIPF table: TurboPack scalar 11694 MB/s encode / 8876 decode vs Simple-8b 848 / 3832; TurboPackV sse 17357 / 12363; TurboVByte 11191 / 10333 vs FP_VByte 5200 / 4268. Ratios (derived from page data): TurboPackV decode ~3.2x Simple-8b, TurboVByte decode ~2.4x FP_VByte. Compression ratio of TurboPack equals fixed-width packing (25.0%) and Simple-8b is 24.0%, so Simple-8b packs slightly smaller there.
stars_or_usage: 848 stars; used by Debian Code Search
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 (commercial license offered by author), so copyleft; C library with C++ headers; SSE/AVX2/NEON/Power9 paths; direct access to bit-packed entries without decompression; no input validation promised beyond 'normally does not read outside buffers'.
caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); README table gives no CPU or flags (the README links an issue titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2' whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags), and the table is labelled 2019.11. Compiler flags unstated, so not tier A. Self-reported 'No other Integer Compression compress/decompress faster' is marketing wording. FastPFor rows use partly 64Ki blocks marked with (*).
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ SIMD integer compression bit packing faster than FastPFor varint github'; then opened the repo README

compiler_and_flags: Release CMake build; compiler and flags not stated
name: VTEnc
baseline: FastPFor, BinaryPacking, VariableByte, VarIntGB (sorted-list integer codecs)
workload: Sorted timestamp list ts.txt (text file of timestamps) and gov2.sorted, encode and decode speed and compression ratio on an i7-6700HQ
claimed_speedup: ts.txt: VTEnc/1 102.28 G/s encode, 7.32 G/s decode, ratio 26,622 vs Delta+FastPFor256 1.45 G/s / 3.61 G/s, ratio 489.4 and Delta+VariableByte 3.89 G/s / 3.43 G/s, ratio 4.0 (derived from page data: ~70x encode and ~2.0x decode vs FastPFor256). gov2.sorted: VTEnc/1 gives the best ratio (8.29) but decodes at 210.99 M/s, far slower than Delta+BinaryPacking 2.33 G/s.
tradeoffs: Cluster-based encoding for sorted integer sets, not a bit-packer; the repo warns the format may change dramatically between versions; encoder can be very slow on gov2.
caveats: Speed win holds only on the highly regular timestamp file; on gov2.sorted it is slower than all bit-packing and varint baselines but compresses best. The author runs the shootout. Compiler flags unstated. Tangential to bit-packing, kept because it is compared directly to FastPFor/BinaryPacking/VByte.

hardware: 8-core Intel i9-9900KF 3.60 GHz, 64 GiB RAM, Linux 5.19.0
tradeoffs: C++ wavelet matrix with 4-ary tree and quad vectors; CMake build, test programs only (test_qvector, test_qwm), no installable library API seen. In the Rust companion table, Qwt256 uses less memory than SDSL (4616 vs 6089 MiB).
caveats: Numbers for this C++ code are not on the README page (only the factor of about 2); I did not open the benchmark program or the paper (arXiv blocked), so tier A rests on the stated compiler, flags and CPU plus public code. Last commit is a README edit from 2023-02-21; the Rust companion is the maintained one.
name: quad-wavelet-tree (C++ QWT)
workload: Access, rank and select latency of a 4-ary wavelet matrix on text (details in the paper arXiv 2302.09239).
claimed_speedup: README: 'improve the latency of access, rank and select queries by factor of ≈ 2' compared to the wavelet trees in SDSL. The README has no table; the matching Rust table (SDSL 1178/1223/2900 ns vs Qwt256 584/613/1623 ns) is at the Rust repo.
found_via: Linked from the QWT Rust README (WebSearch: 'wavelet tree OR wavelet matrix library faster than SDSL github benchmark C++')

hardware: Intel i9-9900KF 3.60 GHz, 64 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 23.04 kernel 6.2.0
tradeoffs: 4-ary wavelet matrix halves cache misses. Rust library, not directly callable from C++ (a C++ port exists as a separate entry). Prefetch (Pfs) variants cost extra space. Huffman variants (HQwt) are smaller and faster but only for skewed alphabets.
caveats: SDSL numbers are measured by the authors, in a C++ run on one machine against Rust implementation numbers; the README says other machines are in the paper (arXiv 2302.09239, blocked). Rank results depend on how query symbols are drawn (frequency-weighted here). Latency (dependent queries), not throughput.
name: QWT (Rust quad wavelet tree)
baseline: SDSL 2.1.1 wavelet matrix/tree (also Pasta, sucds, simple-sds)
workload: Access, rank and select latency on the 4 GiB prefix of Big English (Gutenberg ASCII text, 168 symbols), 10M dependent random queries, single thread.
claimed_speedup: README table: SDSL 2.1.1 access 1178 / rank 1223 / select 2900 ns vs Qwt256 584 / 613 / 1623 ns (about 2x, 2x, 1.8x); Qwt256Pfs rank 434 ns; HQwt256Pfs rank 263 ns, select 952 ns. Space: SDSL 6089 MiB vs Qwt256 4616 MiB.
found_via: WebSearch: 'wavelet tree OR wavelet matrix library faster than SDSL github benchmark C++' (arXiv 2302.09239 Faster Wavelet Tree Queries)

tradeoffs: Entropy-compressed bitvectors (RRR family) trading code complexity for decode speed. Research code: one hybrid variant (hyb_256) is marked broken and debugging code remains.
caveats: Paper (Dönges and Puglisi, SEA 2025) is peer-reviewed but blocked here; speedup magnitude not verified (snippet only for the claim). No LICENSE file found (raw 404), so reference only. README has no performance numbers, flags or CPU.
name: h0_bv (H0-compressed bitvectors)
workload: Access and rank on H0-compressed bitvectors with alternative block decoding and code assignment, benchmarked on web and DNA data (WT-WEB-1GB, WT-DNA-1GB) using code adapted from SDSL rrr_time_and_space.cpp.
claimed_speedup: No numbers seen. Search snippet of the SEA 2025 paper 'Succinct Rank Dictionaries Revisited' says non-lexicographical block codes 'can lead to faster query times and offer relevant space-time trade-offs'.
found_via: WebSearch: '"Succinct Rank Dictionaries Revisited" SEA 2025 github code'

hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2407 v2 2.40GHz, 41 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04.6
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 that depends on SDSL headers. Compressed (space-saving) rather than a pure speed structure; supports operator[], lower_bound, rank, select, iterators, serialization. The experiment repo is GPL-3.0 and needs at least 32 GB RAM and a Google Drive dataset.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (ALENEX 2021, ACM TALG 2022) but I could not open either paper (ACM blocked), and neither README gives speedup numbers, so the claimed advantage over SDSL is unverified here. The tier B rests on peer review only. Baselines named from the experiment repo README.
name: LA-vector
baseline: SDSL compressed bitvectors (sdsl::s18_vector, sdsl::rle_vector and other rank/select dictionaries compared in the paper repo)
workload: Random access and rank over compressed bitvectors/containers using learned piecewise linear approximations; experiments in the paper repo.
claimed_speedup: No numbers seen. The ALENEX 2021 paper title says a learned approach to 'quicken and compress' rank/select dictionaries; the ACM TALG 2022 paper is cited in the README.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Theory Meets Practice for Bit Vectors Supporting Rank and Select github code' (result gvinciguerra/la_vector); experiment repo opened on github.com

tradeoffs: Smaller than the smallest known rank/select structures, but this is a space result; query speed relative to pasta-flat/cs-poppy is not established here.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (SEA 2025, Elias-Fano Compression for Space-Efficient Rank and Select Structures) but the paper is blocked; numbers are from a search snippet only (snippet only). No LICENSE file (raw 404), README is one line, so reference only. Baseline is not SDSL or sux, and the win is space, not speed; included as a related research item.
name: orzo (Elias-Fano encoded L2 rank/select)
workload: Rank and select on bit vectors with Elias-Fano compressed L2 indices to cut index space below the 3.51% of cs-poppy and pasta-flat.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 'Orzo achieves 26.49% space saving over existing state-of-the-art structures like cs-poppy and pasta-flat'. No speed claim seen.
found_via: WebSearch: '"Elias-Fano Compression for Space-Efficient Rank and Select Structures" github code'

hardware: 6-core Intel i7-10750H fixed at 3.0 GHz (FM-index benchmark)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2; gains come from batching and prefetching, so single dependent queries gain less. Rust API with packed u64 input, unsafe unchecked ranks. Not directly usable from C++.
caveats: Paper (SEA 2026, arXiv 2602.04103) and the blog are blocked here; claim text from the repo README and a search snippet. Not shown to be faster than SDSL or sux directly; the baselines are other rank implementations (qwt, etc.), so baseline_in_list=false. No LICENSE file; MIT comes from Cargo.toml. Benchmark commands are in the README but plots only, no numbers.
name: QuadRank / BiRank
baseline: Other binary and DNA rank structures (the README plots include qwt RSQ256/RSQ512; names of the remaining baselines are only in the paper and plots); for FM-index: genedex and AWRY
workload: Rank over bit vectors and 2-bit DNA text under batched and prefetched queries (1, 6 and 12 threads); FM-index count-only mapping of simulated 150bp reads (1% error) against a 3.1 Gbp human genome with 12 threads.
claimed_speedup: README: BiRank and QuadRank are 'up to 2x faster than other methods in high-throughput settings'; QuadFm is 'up to 4x faster than genedex'. Space overhead 3.28% (BiRank) and 14.4% (QuadRank) per paper snippet. No numeric table in the README (plots only).
found_via: WebSearch: 'SPIDER succinct rank select github Laws ...' result 'QuadRank: Engineering a High Throughput Rank'; 'QuadRank high throughput rank github RagnarGrootKoerkamp quadrank'

tradeoffs: Interleaves rank metadata with the bit vector (single cache miss per rank); select uses a prediction model. C code is a set of standalone test executables (spider.c, ni-spider.c, select variants), not a library API.
caveats: Peer-reviewed at SEA 2024, but the paper (dagstuhl, arXiv) is blocked here, so the claim text is from a WebSearch snippet only (snippet only). The repo README has no benchmark numbers, flags or CPU and no LICENSE file was found (raw LICENSE 404), so code must not be copied. Benefit is for very large vectors.
name: SPIDER (Succinct Predictive InDEx for Rank and select)
baseline: SDSL rank/select; also compared against less space-efficient rank structures (competitors named in the paper, not opened)
workload: Rank and select queries on large bit vectors (datasets of 8 billion or more bits are where the rank win is reported).
claimed_speedup: Snippet of arXiv 2405.05214 abstract: 3.82% extra space and 'the best known rank query time for data sets of 8 billion or more bits, even compared to much less space-efficient data structures'; select uses predictions to nearly eliminate the linear scan. No ratio seen.
found_via: WebSearch: 'succinct rank select bit vector paper faster than SDSL sux' then 'SPIDER succinct rank select github Laws bit vector SEA 2024 code'

hardware: Apple Silicon M-series (exact chip not stated)
tradeoffs: Header-only. Tuned for ARM64: 4096/256-bit asymmetric blocks and select sampling every 256th set bit. RRRBitVec is entropy compressed but slow on rank (9.39 ns). Build time of FastBitVec about 330 ms at 100M bits.
caveats: Single-author preprint (arXiv 2605.25528, not peer reviewed; arXiv blocked, read via repo README only). Single size N=1M only in the headline table, which fits in cache; exact CPU model missing, so tier C not A. SDSL select number is for select_support_mcl by build option; SDSL rank_support_v is not the fastest SDSL rank (v5 has less space), and sux/pasta were not compared. Correctness fuzzer with 78M assertions is included.
name: succinct-bitvec-cpp (FastBitVec / RRRBitVec)
workload: Rank and select on a 1,000,000-bit vector, 50% density, uniform random queries, Google Benchmark mean latency.
claimed_speedup: README table: FastBitVec rank 1.65 ns vs SDSL rank_support_v 2.25 ns (about 1.36x, derived from page data); select 44.5 ns vs SDSL 78.4 ns (about 1.76x, derived from page data); RRRBitVec select 33.7 ns. Total space 1.141 bpe vs SDSL 1.250 bpe.
found_via: WebSearch: 'FastBitVec succinct bit vector ARM64 github' (result: arXiv 2605.25528 Engineering Practical Succinct Bit Vectors ... Apple Silicon)
